Cohen's d

title: Systematic Desensitization vs. Exposure Therapy
html:
Systematic Desensitization vs. Exposure Therapy
Systematic Desensitization
  • Wolpe (1958)
  • Mechanism: counterconditioning
  • Principle: reciprocal inhibition
  • Pairs CS with deep relaxation
  • Uses graded fear hierarchy
  • Replaces fear CR with calm CR
  • Typically imaginal exposure
Exposure Therapy
  • Craske et al. (2014)
  • Mechanism: extinction learning
  • Principle: inhibitory learning
  • CS presented without US
  • Multiple contexts recommended
  • Expectancy violation is key
  • In vivo & imaginal exposure

title: CTT vs. IRT: Key Framework Contrasts
html:
CTT vs. IRT: Key Framework Contrasts
Classical Test Theory (CTT)
  • Analyzes total test scores
  • Item stats depend on sample tested
  • Ability estimates depend on which test given
  • Single SEM for all examinees
  • Simple formula: X = T + E
  • Reliability = proportion of true score variance
Item Response Theory (IRT)
  • Analyzes individual items
  • Item parameters are sample-independent
  • Ability estimates are test-independent
  • Unique SEM at each ability level
  • Models probability of correct response
  • Enables CAT and item banking

title: IRT Models: 1PL, 2PL, and 3PL
html:

3PL Model
Difficulty (b) + Discrimination (a) + Guessing (c) — accounts for correct guessing; most common for standardized multiple-choice tests
2PL Model
Difficulty (b) + Discrimination (a) — items vary in steepness of ICC; more realistic for many tests
1PL Rasch Model
Difficulty (b) only — all items equally discriminating; no guessing; simplest model; emphasizes specific objectivity

title: Predictive vs. Concurrent Validity Comparison
html:
Predictive vs. Concurrent Validity Comparison
Predictive Validity
  • Criterion measured later in time
  • Goal: forecast future outcomes
  • Sample: applicants or candidates
  • Used for selection and admissions
  • Limitation: time delay, attrition
  • Example: GRE predicting 1st-year GPA
Concurrent Validity
  • Criterion measured simultaneously
  • Goal: substitute for existing measure
  • Sample: current group members
  • Used for screening and diagnosis
  • Limitation: may not generalize to prediction
  • Example: new depression screen vs. established interview

title: Standard Error of Estimate: Validity and Prediction Precision

title: Sensitivity vs. Specificity Cutoff Trade-offs

Lower Cutoff

Higher Cutoff

  • Sensitivity decreases
  • Best when false alarms are costly (e.g., stigmatizing diagnosis)

title: Probability vs. Nonprobability Sampling Methods
html:
Probability vs. Nonprobability Sampling Methods
Probability Sampling
  • Every member has known, nonzero selection chance
  • Supports statistical generalization to population
  • Simple Random — equal chance, unbiased
  • Stratified Random — ensures subgroup representation
  • Cluster — selects groups, practical for dispersed populations
  • Systematic — every kth member from a list
Nonprobability Sampling
  • No guarantee of known selection probability
  • Limits formal statistical generalization
  • Convenience — readily available participants
  • Purposive — handpicked for specific characteristics
  • Snowball — participants recruit from social networks
  • Best for exploratory, qualitative, hidden populations

Types of External Validity Threats

Setting × Treatment

Threats to External Validity

title: Threats to Construct Validity in Research
html:
Threats to Construct Validity in Research
Inadequate Explication

Construct poorly defined; operationalization misses key dimensions or drifts into another construct

Mono-Operation Bias

Single operationalization of construct; captures only part, misses full dimensionality

Mono-Method Bias

All measures use same method (e.g., self-report only); shared variance inflates relationships

Hypothesis Guessing

Demand characteristics; participants alter behavior based on guessed purpose

Experimenter Expectancy

Researcher expectations bias administration or scoring; solved by double-blind design

Confounding

Two constructs bundled together; cannot isolate which produced the effect

Random Selection

  • Creates representative samples
  • Supports generalizability of findings
  • Required for population validity

title: Convergent vs. Discriminant Validity — MTMM Logic
html:
Convergent vs. Discriminant Validity — MTMM Logic
Convergent Validity
  • High correlations with measures of the SAME construct
  • Monotrait-heteromethod cells in MTMM
  • Supports that the test measures the intended attribute
  • Example: new depression scale correlates r = .82 with established BDI-II
Discriminant Validity
  • Low correlations with measures of DIFFERENT constructs
  • Heterotrait-monomethod cells in MTMM
  • Supports distinctiveness of the measured construct
  • Example: depression scale shows low correlation with unrelated constructs (e.g., spatial ability)

  • Example: Social support buffers stress–depression relationship

Stage 1

Anger — "Why me? This isn't fair!" Rage directed at doctors, family, or universe; reflects sense of injustice.
Stage 3
Bargaining — "If I could just have more time..." Negotiating with fate or higher power for more time or a cure.
Stage 4
Depression — Mourning impending losses. Reactive (losses experienced) vs. preparatory (anticipatory grief).
Stage 5
Acceptance — At peace with reality of death; quiet, reflective, focused on goodbyes.
Key Critique
Not a fixed sequence — Stages are not universal, not always in order, may overlap or be skipped. Best understood as common reactions, not a prescriptive progression.

title: Extinction Process: From Burst to Recovery
html:
Extinction Process: From Burst to Recovery
Baseline
Behavior is consistently reinforced — child tantrums, parent gives candy. Behavior maintained at stable rate.
Extinction Begins
Reinforcement is withheld. Behavior that previously "worked" no longer produces the expected consequence.
Extinction Burst
Temporary spike in frequency, intensity, or variability of behavior. If caregiver gives in here, a more intense behavior is intermittently reinforced — making extinction harder.
Behavior Declines
Continued non-reinforcement leads to gradual reduction. CRF-trained behaviors extinguish faster than intermittently reinforced ones (PREE).
Spontaneous Recovery
After a rest period, extinguished behavior may temporarily reappear. Continued non-reinforcement produces rapid re-extinction. Does not mean extinction failed.

title: Stages of Change: Matched Processes & Interventions
html:
Stages of Change: Matched Processes & Interventions
Precontemplation
Not yet considering change — unaware or in denial. Best matched: consciousness raising, dramatic relief, environmental reevaluation. Avoid: self-liberation, stimulus control.
Contemplation
Aware but ambivalent — weighing pros and cons; may persist for years. Best matched: self-reevaluation, consciousness raising, decisional balance. Avoid: self-liberation (premature commitment).
Preparation
Intending to act soon; making small preliminary steps. Best matched: self-liberation, self-reevaluation. Ambivalence largely resolved.
Action
Actively modifying behavior; high commitment required. Best matched: counterconditioning, stimulus control, reinforcement management.
Maintenance
Sustaining change; preventing relapse. Best matched: helping relationships, stimulus control, counterconditioning.

Confirmation Bias — selectively attend to, encode, and recall information that confirms the activated schema; ambiguous evidence interpreted as supporting

Premature diagnostic closure — initial impression anchors all subsequent judgment; contradictory findings discounted or overlooked

title: Delirium vs. Dementia: Key Distinguishing Features

  • Fluctuating course, worse at night
  • Attention severely impaired (hallmark)
  • Consciousness clouded/altered
  • Visual hallucinations common
  • Usually reversible if cause treated
  • Causes: infection, withdrawal, metabolic, toxins
Dementia (Major NCD)
  • Insidious onset (months to years)
  • Progressive, stable day-to-day
  • Attention relatively preserved until late
  • Consciousness clear until late stages
  • Hallucinations less common (except DLB)
  • Usually irreversible and progressive
  • Pre-existing dementia is a delirium risk factor

title: Phases of the Action Potential
html:
Phases of the Action Potential
Resting State
Membrane potential: -70 mV. Na+/K+ pump maintains gradient. Na+ outside, K+ inside.
Threshold Reached
Depolarization to -55 mV triggers action potential. All-or-none — fires fully or not at all.
Depolarization
Voltage-gated Na+ channels open. Rapid Na+ influx. Membrane peaks at +30 to +40 mV.
Repolarization
Na+ channels inactivate. K+ channels open. K+ efflux returns membrane toward -70 mV. Absolute refractory period.
Hyperpolarization
K+ channels stay open briefly. Membrane overshoots to ~-80 mV. Relative refractory period — stronger stimulus needed.
Resting Restored
K+ channels close. Na+/K+ pump restores -70 mV. Neuron ready to fire again.

anchor_heading: Standard Error of Measurement & Confidence Intervals
title: SEM, Sdiff, and SEE: Three Error Concepts
html:
SEM, Sdiff, and SEE: Three Error Concepts
SEM
  • Standard Error of Measurement
  • Formula: SD × sqrt(1 − rxx)
  • Uses reliability coefficient
  • Precision of a single observed score
  • Builds confidence intervals around one score
  • 68% CI = score ± 1 SEM
  • 95% CI = score ± 1.96 SEM
Sdiff
  • Standard Error of the Difference
  • Formula: sqrt(SEM1² + SEM2²)
  • Uses two SEMs combined
  • Precision of a discrepancy between two scores
  • Determines if score difference is significant
  • Significant if discrepancy > 1.96 × Sdiff
  • Also used in Reliable Change Index
SEE
  • Standard Error of Estimate
  • Formula: SDY × sqrt(1 − rxy²)
  • Uses validity coefficient
  • Precision of a predicted score (regression)
  • Applies to prediction from one measure to another
  • Smaller when validity is higher
  • Analogous to SEM but for predicted values

title: Reliable Change: From Measurement Error to Clinical Significance
html:
Reliable Change: From Measurement Error to Clinical Significance
Compute SEM
SD × sqrt(1 − rxx)
Reflects test reliability
→
Compute Sdiff
sqrt(2 × SEM²)
Combines error across two time points
→
Compute RCI
(X2 − X1) / Sdiff
RCI > 1.96 = reliable change at .05

Assess Clinical Significance

title: EPS Types: Onset Timeline & Key Features
html:
EPS Types: Onset Timeline & Key Features
Hours to Days
Acute Dystonia — Sustained muscle contractions: torticollis, oculogyric crisis, opisthotonus. Young males at highest risk. Treat with anticholinergics (benztropine, diphenhydramine IM).
Days to Weeks
Akathisia — Inner restlessness, inability to sit still. Often mistaken for worsening psychosis. Treat with beta-blockers (propranolol) or benzodiazepines — NOT anticholinergics.
Weeks to Months
Drug-Induced Parkinsonism — Bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, resting tremor, shuffling gait, mask-like facies. Treat with anticholinergics (benztropine) or amantadine.
Months to Years
Tardive Dyskinesia — Involuntary orofacial movements: lip smacking, tongue protrusion, grimacing. May be irreversible. Worsens paradoxically if drug abruptly stopped. Treat with VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine).

title: CYP450 Inhibitors vs. Inducers: Clinical Impact
html:
CYP450 Inhibitors vs. Inducers: Clinical Impact
CYP450 Inhibitor
  • Slows metabolism of substrate
  • Substrate levels increase
  • Risk: toxicity
  • Examples: fluoxetine, paroxetine (CYP2D6); fluvoxamine (CYP1A2, CYP3A4); ketoconazole, grapefruit juice (CYP3A4)
  • Clinical case: fluoxetine + haloperidol → raised haloperidol → EPS risk
  • Onset: rapid (within days)
CYP450 Inducer
  • Speeds up metabolism of substrate
  • Substrate levels decrease
  • Risk: therapeutic failure
  • Examples: carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's Wort (CYP3A4); smoking/tobacco (CYP1A2)
  • Clinical case: carbamazepine + oral contraceptives → contraceptive failure
  • Onset: gradual (days to weeks)

title: Drug-Receptor Agonism Spectrum
html:
Drug-Receptor Agonism Spectrum
Inverse Agonist
Binds receptor; produces effect opposite to agonist; reduces activity below baseline (e.g., some beta-carbolines at GABA-A)
Antagonist
Binds receptor; blocks activation; zero intrinsic activity; no effect alone (e.g., haloperidol at D2)
Partial Agonist
Binds and activates; submaximal response; stabilizing effect — agonist in low-NT states, antagonist in high-NT states (e.g., aripiprazole at D2; buspirone at 5-HT1A)
Full Agonist
Binds and fully activates receptor; maximal response; mimics endogenous neurotransmitter (e.g., benzodiazepines at GABA-A)

title: GABA-A vs. GABA-B: Mechanism & Drug Targets
html:
GABA-A vs. GABA-B: Mechanism & Drug Targets
GABA-A
  • Ionotropic (ligand-gated Cl- channel)
  • GABA opens channel → hyperpolarization
  • Benzodiazepines: increase opening frequency
  • Barbiturates: increase opening duration
  • Zolpidem: binds alpha-1 subunit selectively
  • Benzos are positive allosteric modulators — require GABA to work
  • Barbiturate OD more dangerous (can open channel without GABA)
GABA-B
  • Metabotropic (G-protein coupled)
  • Increases K+ conductance, inhibits Ca2+ channels
  • Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist
  • Used for muscle relaxation & alcohol use disorder (off-label)
  • NOT affected by benzodiazepines

title: Stimulants vs. Atomoxetine: ADHD Pharmacotherapy

Stimulants vs. Atomoxetine: ADHD Pharmacotherapy
Stimulants (Schedule II)
  • Methylphenidate, Amphetamines, Lisdexamfetamine
  • Block DA & NE reuptake; amphetamines also promote release
  • First-line treatment for ADHD
  • Rapid onset — effect within hours
  • Abuse potential; controlled substance
  • Vyvanse (prodrug) reduces abuse risk
  • Side effects: appetite loss, insomnia, elevated BP/HR
  • Non-ADHD users: improved subjective focus but no GPA gain
Atomoxetine (Strattera)
  • Selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (NRI)
  • Not a controlled substance — no abuse potential
  • Preferred for comorbid SUD or anxiety
  • Slow onset — 4 to 6 weeks for full effect
  • 24-hour continuous coverage
  • Less effective than stimulants for many patients
  • Black box warning: suicidal ideation in youth
  • Rare hepatotoxicity risk

title: Forensic vs. Therapeutic Role Contrast
html:
Forensic vs. Therapeutic Role Contrast
Therapeutic Role
  • Primary allegiance: client welfare
  • Built on empathy & trust
  • Advocate for client
  • Confidentiality protects client
  • Voluntary participation by client
  • Present- & future-focused
  • Goal: healing & wellbeing
Forensic Role
  • Primary allegiance: legal system / truth
  • Built on impartiality & objectivity
  • No advocacy — neutral evaluator
  • Results shared with court/attorneys
  • Examinee often compelled to participate
  • Past-focused (insanity) or present-focused (competency)
  • Goal: accurate information for legal process
